胡主任.note: An officer of the Juntong headquarters inspectorate in Chongqing who sets Lin to watch Gu Shenyan. A fictional character; surname romanized.

潘新民.note: Old Pan's full name, given under interrogation; code name Index Finger. Pinyin.

荣将军.note: A general of the Nationalist Ministry of National Defense's Operations Department; a Communist agent, his home name Liu Zongming. Surname romanized.

刘宗铭.note: General Rong's name in his native place; he and Old Pan served together in the Nineteenth Route Army. Pinyin.

子璐.note: Miss Lan's son, killed in a stray-bullet crossfire. Pinyin of his given name.

黎广文.note: Meng Annan's cover name in postwar Shanghai, working as an editor at the French Photo Agency; Zhu Yizhen passes in cover as his wife, Mrs. Li. Pinyin.

阮志中.note: Meng Annan's true Vietnamese name; his parents, followers of Ho Chi Minh, died in a French prison in Saigon. Vietnamese form (Nguyễn Chí Trung).

胡志明.note: Historical (1890–1969); Vietnamese revolutionary, later president of North Vietnam. Standard English form.

保密局.note: The postwar reorganization of the Juntong. Romanized abbreviation, kept distinct from its wartime predecessor.

忠义救国军.note: Dai Li's guerrilla and paramilitary force. Attested English name.

力行社.note: The secret inner core of the Blue Shirts, tied to Dai Li. Attested romanization.

中央银行.note: The Nationalist government's central bank; not to be confused with the Wang regime's Central Reserve Bank. Attested English name.

华东局.note: The Chinese Communist Party's regional bureau for East China. Attested English name.

东方通讯社.note: A news agency Lin heads in cover in postwar Shanghai.

十九路军.note: The Nationalist army that defended Shanghai against Japan in 1932. Attested English name.

旅欧中国少年共产党.en: the Chinese Youth Communist Party in Europe
旅欧中国少年共产党.note: The European branch of the early Chinese Communist movement, founded in Paris in 1922. Attested English rendering.

三野.note: One of the People's Liberation Army's field armies in the civil war. Attested English name.

志愿军.note: The Chinese People's Volunteer Army sent to fight in the Korean War. Attested English name.

歌乐山.note: The hills west of Chongqing where the Juntong and SACO kept training grounds and a prison. Attested romanization.

嘉陵江.note: The river that joins the Yangtze at Chongqing. Attested English form.

延安.note: The Communists' wartime capital in northern Shaanxi. Attested pinyin.

斜塘镇.note: A small water-country town on the outskirts of Shanghai where Lin hides as a schoolteacher. Pinyin.

静安寺.note: A famous ancient Buddhist temple in central Shanghai; the district and road bear its name. Attested English form.

爱丁堡大厦.note: An apartment building beside the Jing'an Temple; Lin's Shanghai residence. Rendered by the English place-name in the source.

兆丰公园.note: A western-Shanghai park, known in English as Jessfield Park, today's Zhongshan Park. Romanized from the Chinese name.

百乐门.note: The celebrated Art Deco dance hall of 1930s–40s Shanghai. Attested English name (百乐门 transliterates 'Paramount').

丹桂戏园.note: A long-established Shanghai opera house. Attested romanization.

西柏坡.note: The Hebei village that served as the Communist central headquarters in 1948. Attested pinyin.

富阳.note: A district of Hangzhou, Zhejiang; Lin's claimed native place under his alias. Attested pinyin.

督邮街.note: The busiest night district of wartime Chongqing. Pinyin.

金都大戏院.note: A cinema on Avenue Foch in Shanghai; the site of the military-police gunfight. Rendered by the theater's period English name.

福熙路.note: A French Concession boulevard, today's central Yan'an Middle Road. Attested French name.

圣类思中学.note: A Catholic mission school in Xietang where Lin teaches (类思 renders the Christian name Aloysius).

南宁.note: The capital of Guangxi, in the region where Ho Chi Minh was jailed by the Nationalists. Attested pinyin.

忘忧清乐集.note: A Song-dynasty classic of go; here it doubles as the key text of a cipher. Attested romanization.

汉奸.note: Literally a traitor to the Han, i.e. a collaborator with the Japanese; the postwar treason trials pursued them. Rendered 'traitor / collaborator' by context.

食指.note: Old Pan's code name; literally the index finger (the 'eating finger'). Rendered by sense.

ch08.note: Mount Gele (歌乐山), in the hills west of Chongqing, was where the Nationalists and the joint Sino-American organization kept training grounds, offices, and a notorious secret prison. Historical.

ch08.anchor: peaches and plums fill the world
ch08.note: The idiom is 桃李满天下, literally “peaches and plums fill all under heaven”: a teacher's pupils (his “peaches and plums”) are everywhere, a tribute to how widely he has taught. Here it flatters Gu Shenyan, whose students reach even into the highest ranks.

ch08.anchor: the Eighth Route Army office at No. 50 Zengjiayan
ch08.note: Zengjiayan No. 50 (曾家岩50号) was the Communists' liaison office in wartime Chongqing, associated with Zhou Enlai and the Party's Southern Bureau; it operated openly during the united front against Japan and was kept under close Nationalist surveillance. Historical.

ch08.anchor: Song-dynasty printing of the Wangyou Qingle Ji
ch08.note: The Wangyou Qingle Ji (忘忧清乐集, “Collection of Pure Joy in Forgetting Cares”) is a Song-dynasty classic of go, among the oldest surviving printed go treatises, gathering opening patterns and endgame problems. Corroborated (its Song origin, c. 1100, is attested in Chinese and Western scholarship). Here it serves as the key text of a cipher. On go itself, see the earlier note.

The Japanese terror-bombing of Chongqing ran from 1938 to 1943 and ended with a final raid on 23 August 1943; the date is corroborated. The specific figure of fifty-four aircraft flying from Wuhan is the novel's, and could not be independently confirmed against the scholarship on the campaign.

ch08.anchor: gone to Yan'an, or to Nanjing
ch08.note: The two enemy destinations: Yan'an (延安), the Communists' wartime capital in northern Shaanxi, and Nanjing, the seat of Wang Jingwei's Japanese-sponsored government. For a Juntong man to defect to either would ruin both Gu and the officer set to watch him.

ch08.anchor: the Chinese Youth Communist Party in Europe
ch08.note: The Chinese Youth Communist Party (旅欧中国少年共产党), founded in Paris in 1922 by work-study students including Zhou Enlai and Zhao Shiyan, was the European branch that helped seed the Chinese Communist Party. Historical.

The Whampoa Military Academy (黄埔军校), founded near Guangzhou in 1924 with Chiang Kai-shek as commandant, trained the officer corps of both the Nationalist and (in its early united-front years) the Communist armies. Historical.

ch08.anchor: both Eastern Expeditions and in the Northern Expedition
ch08.note: The Eastern Expeditions (1925) crushed the warlord Chen Jiongming in Guangdong; the Northern Expedition (1926–1928) was the Nationalist campaign that defeated the northern warlords and nominally reunified China. Historical.

The purge (清党) of 1927, begun with Chiang Kai-shek's violent April 12 coup in Shanghai, expelled and massacred Communists within the Nationalist camp and ended the first united front. To “break with the Chinese Communists” then was to change sides in a bloodletting. Historical.

ch08.anchor: followed Dai Li into the Lixingshe
ch08.note: The Lixingshe (力行社, the “Vigorous Practice Society”), founded 1932, was the secret, fascist-influenced inner core of Chiang Kai-shek's loyalist organization and the seedbed of Dai Li's secret service; it stood at the center of the wider Blue Shirts (see the earlier note). Historical.

ch08.anchor: now called himself Ho Chi Minh
ch08.note: Ho Chi Minh (1890–1969), the Vietnamese revolutionary and future president of North Vietnam, used many names across his career, among them Nguyen Ai Quoc and Ho Quang; he adopted the name Ho Chi Minh around the time of his release. He was in fact imprisoned by Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists in Guangxi from August 1942 to September 1943, moved through many jails — so Gu's clandestine prison visit is grounded in real history. Corroborated. On the Indochinese Communist Party, see the earlier note.

ch08.anchor: our Expeditionary Force in the Burma-India theater
ch08.note: The Chinese Expeditionary Force fought the Japanese in Burma alongside British and American troops (1942, and again 1943–1945) to keep open China's overland supply lines. Historical.

ch08.anchor: a plum-blossom brand, with no second hand
ch08.note: The watch's brand is 梅花, “plum blossom” — the same flower as the cipher poem “Ode to the Plum Blossom” noted earlier, and Gu's recurring emblem. Its missing second hand quietly marks a man whose own time is running out.

ch09.note: Nylon stockings (玻璃丝袜, literally “glass-silk stockings”) were a coveted American luxury in wartime China, along with the chocolate — the small tribute the foreign officers paid the women they took.

ch09.anchor: roving orioles of the low song halls
ch09.note: The phrase is 流莺, “roving oriole,” an old literary euphemism for a streetwalker: a woman who solicits on the move, as the bird flits from branch to branch.

The idiom is 车水马龙, “carriages like flowing water, horses like a dragon”: a scene of dense, ceaseless traffic. The natural English keeps the bustle; the image is the coiling dragon of an unbroken line of horses.
The Central Bank of China (中央银行) was the Nationalist government's own central bank, not to be confused with the Wang Jingwei regime's Central Reserve Bank noted earlier. Historical.
A 牌楼 (or 牌坊): a free-standing ceremonial gateway of stone or wood, raised to mark a temple, a street, or an act of virtue. A fixture of the old Chinese townscape.

ch10.anchor: the campaign to punish the traitors
ch10.note: A 汉奸 (hànjiān) is a “traitor to the Han,” a Chinese who collaborated with the Japanese occupier; after the 1945 victory the Nationalist government tried and executed collaborators in a wave of treason cases. The word is distinct from the 叛逆者 of the novel's title, discussed in an earlier note. Historical.
The Jing'an Temple (静安寺), an ancient Buddhist temple in central Shanghai; the surrounding district and its main road take their name from it. Historical.

The Loyal and Patriotic Army (忠义救国军), formed by Dai Li in 1937 and later trained under the Sino-American Cooperative Organization, was the Juntong's guerrilla and paramilitary arm; its units were among the first Nationalist troops to enter Shanghai after the Japanese surrender. Corroborated.
The Chongqing negotiations of 1945 between the Nationalists and the Communists, which produced the “Double Tenth Agreement” but failed to avert the civil war. Historical.

ch10.anchor: two grasshoppers tied to one string
ch10.note: The idiom is 一条绳上的蚂蚱, “grasshoppers strung on one line”: two parties so bound together that neither can escape the other's fate. The image is of insects tied to a single thread — one jumps, both go.
Wartime Shanghai and the towns around it sheltered tens of thousands of European Jewish refugees; the German clinic and its Jewish proprietress-nurse reflect that real presence. Historical.

ch10.anchor: the back gate of Zhaofeng Park
ch10.note: Zhaofeng Park (兆丰公园) was known to foreigners as Jessfield Park — the same Jessfield that named the road where No. 76 stood; it is today's Zhongshan Park in western Shanghai. Corroborated.
Fabi (法币), the Nationalist government's legal-tender paper money, introduced in 1935; by the late 1940s runaway inflation had all but destroyed its value. Historical.
“The old home” (老家) is the underground's code for the Communist base area and Party center — the place an exposed agent is recalled to. It recurs through these chapters as a quiet euphemism.

ch10.anchor: We are here to rescue you
ch10.note: This is the language of the “Rescue Campaign” (抢救运动) of 1943, the coercive spy-hunting phase of the Yan'an Rectification (noted earlier), in which cadres were pressed by interrogation into false confessions of espionage; “rescue” was the campaign's own euphemism for the purge. Zhu is being told her imprisonment is for her own good. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: before you speak, you greet the person first
ch11.note: A child in China is taught to address an elder by the proper kin-title before speaking to them; Miss Lan is coaching her son in the courtesy. His flat “My papa died long ago” is a pointed refusal of it.

ch11.anchor: a wild chicken, an oil-bottle drag, a broom-star
ch11.note: The four insults for a woman like her: 破鞋, a “worn shoe” (a loose or adulterous woman); 野鸡, a “wild chicken” (an unlicensed prostitute); 拖油瓶, an “oil-bottle drag” (a child a woman brings with her into a remarriage, and so the burdened woman herself); 扫帚星, a “broom-star,” that is a comet, a bringer of ruin, a woman blamed for the deaths around her. The English keeps the images; each is a small verdict of the society on her.

ch11.anchor: Mr. Du to be our witness
ch11.note: Du Yuesheng (杜月笙, 1888–1951), boss of the Green Gang and the most powerful private man in Republican Shanghai, patron and power-broker across business, politics, and the underworld. To secure him as a wedding witness is a mark of how far Lin has risen. Historical.
In 1946 the wartime Juntong was reorganized as the Ministry of National Defense's Bureau of Secrecy, the 保密局 (Baomiju), the postwar Nationalist secret service. Historical.

ch11.anchor: sweep your grave, and every day
ch11.note: The rites of the dead: 扫墓, sweeping and tending the grave, especially at the Qingming festival, and 上香, the daily offering of incense. To be left to perform them is, in her vow, the one thing worth living for.

ch11.anchor: the Metropol Theater on Avenue Foch
ch11.note: Avenue Foch (福熙路) was a French Concession boulevard, today's Yan'an Middle Road. The clash the novel stages — between Nationalist military police (宪兵) and the civil police — reflects a real and chronic friction between the two forces in the postwar city, though this particular incident is the novel's own.

The film's title, 龙凤花烛, names the paired dragon-and-phoenix candles burned at a wedding — an emblem of marriage and good fortune, set with deliberate cruelty against the child's death in the same scene.
A 盆景 (penjing): the Chinese art of the miniature tree or landscape grown in a shallow tray, the older cousin of the Japanese bonsai.

ch11.anchor: guard the stump to wait for the hare
ch11.note: The idiom is 守株待兔, from a fable in the Han Feizi: a farmer once saw a hare run headlong into a tree stump and die, and ever after waited by the stump for another — to trust foolishly to luck, or, as here, to lie in wait for the quarry to deliver itself.

ch11.anchor: strike the mountain to startle the tiger
ch11.note: The idiom is 敲山震虎, “strike the mountain to shake the tiger”: to make a show of force at one remove, so as to intimidate an adversary or flush him into the open.

ch11.anchor: the Jiangsu Special Committee's, and the Comintern's
ch11.note: Meng lists the tangle of Communist intelligence lines then running in Shanghai: the Party's East China Bureau (华东局) and Jiangsu Special Committee, the center at Yan'an, and the Comintern — the Moscow-run Communist International. To verify a man across these separate lines risked crossing them and exposing both. Historical.

ch12.note: The word here is 叛徒, a turncoat who betrays his own side and comrades — distinct from the 汉奸 (collaborator with the foreign enemy) noted earlier, and from the 叛逆者 of the title. Old Pan chooses to wear the name of the first so that his mission may live.

ch12.anchor: a shuttle in the Communist intelligence network
ch12.note: The word is 梭子, a weaver's shuttle: a courier who plies back and forth across the network carrying its messages, as the shuttle runs the thread across the loom.

Gu Shunzhang (顾顺章) was the head of the Chinese Communist Party's own security and intelligence service; captured in 1931, he defected to the Nationalists, and his confessions exposed the underground and led to mass arrests, nearly destroying the Party's urban networks. He is the archetype the station chief invokes: the senior agent who sells out his own. Corroborated.

ch12.anchor: beat the grass and startle the snake
ch12.note: The idiom is 打草惊蛇, “beat the grass and startle the snake”: to act rashly and alert the very quarry you meant to take unawares.
The Paramount (百乐门), the great Art Deco dance hall on Bubbling Well Road, was an emblem of Shanghai's glittering nightlife from the 1930s. Historical.

ch13.note: The Dangui (丹桂), one of old Shanghai's celebrated opera houses, its lineage going back to the great teahouse-theaters of the late nineteenth century. Historical.

The Nineteenth Route Army (十九路军) put up the fierce, celebrated defense of Shanghai against the Japanese in the January 28 Incident of 1932. That Rong and Old Pan “resisted the Japanese together in Shanghai” places them in that fight. Historical.

A 义庄: a charitable hall, often maintained by a native-place association or lineage, that housed coffins and corpses awaiting burial or transport back to the dead person's home district — a standard provision for those who died away from home. Historical.

The intelligence Lin carries belongs to the Liaoshen Campaign (September–November 1948), the decisive Manchurian campaign of the civil war. The siege of Changchun (May–October 1948) blockaded and starved the Nationalist garrison into surrender; a deployment-and-reinforcement plan for the Liao–Shen theater was battle-turning material. Corroborated.

ch13.anchor: the Anti-Japanese Military and Political University
ch13.note: Kangda (抗大), the Communists' cadre-training academy at Yan'an, which schooled a generation of Party military and political officers. Historical.

Xibaipo (西柏坡), the village in Hebei that served as the Communist Party's central headquarters in 1948, from which Mao Zedong and the leadership directed the closing campaigns of the civil war. Historical.

ch13.anchor: a hawk Gu Shenyan set loose
ch13.note: The word is 鹞子, a sparrowhawk or falcon; in the trade it is an agent “let loose” to fly free under deep cover for years — the very thing Meng Annan turns out to be.
An 义子: a formally adopted, non-blood son. Gu Shenyan raised Meng Annan after the boy's parents died; Lin was Gu's student, Meng his foster son — “only, each of us chose his own road.”

Meng Annan's true Vietnamese name (阮志中). His parents were followers of Ho Chi Minh who had studied in France, where they met Gu Shenyan, and who died in a French colonial prison in Saigon when the boy was ten. Historical in kind: Vietnamese revolutionaries were widely jailed and killed under French rule in this period.

ch14.note: A Catholic mission school (圣类思中学): 类思 renders the Christian name Aloysius. Such foreign-run mission schools were common in and around Republican Shanghai.

The alias joins Lin's own surname to 秋明 — the given name of Zuo Qiuming (左秋明), the friend and fellow trainee who took his own life under interrogation rather than talk (Batch 1). Lin lives on under the dead man's name. A telling name the Chinese reader catches at once.

ch14.anchor: a village head in the town
ch14.note: A 保长 (baozhang), the headman of a bao — a unit of the old baojia system of mutual-surveillance household groupings, inherited from the Nationalist order and, for a time, kept on after 1949. Here the local baozhang is the informer. Historical.

ch14.anchor: her hair in a child's bob
ch14.note: A 童花头, the girlish “child-flower” bob with a straight fringe — the schoolgirl hairstyle that fixes Zhu Yizhen, in Lin's memory, as the student she was when they met.

ch14.anchor: to Resist America and Aid Korea
ch14.note: The Korean War mobilization: China entered the war in October 1950, and the “Resist America, Aid Korea, Defend Home and Country” (抗美援朝，保家卫国) campaign — with its patriotic donation drives for the Volunteer Army — swept the cities through 1950–1951. Historical.

ch14.anchor: the war of resistance against the French
ch14.note: The First Indochina War (1946–1954), in which Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh fought to end French colonial rule in Vietnam. Meng Annan asks to go home and join it. Historical.

ch14.anchor: the Third Field Army to the Fujian front
ch14.note: The People's Liberation Army's Third Field Army carried the civil war into the southeast in 1949, including the Fujian coast facing Taiwan. Historical.
